I loved this game! I found it very interesting to see which weird conclusions you can have from just snippets of information.  Very hot topic and for me a confirmation why I'm against governments who want to track your information online.

Do you ever just want to snoop in other people's social lives and mess around with their personal life, Exposing Criminals and dealing justice by presenting said evidence to the media? Have you ever wondered how rich or poor some people's bank accounts are? Do you also gain the satisfaction that you are literally everywhere in the online world, in PCs and Cellphones?

Well this game is for you.

The story is well written, the mechanics are easily understandble [i]atleast in my own gameplay [/i], It's also tackles one of the world's real life problems in how the Government tries to protect you by invading your privacy. Although it is a short game, you could probably beat it in 2 - 4 hours max, I'd still say you should get it, even if it is a short story game.

So I picked this game up on HumbleBundle a good while back and completely forgot to ever install or play it. I just discovered it today and holy crap, this game is a masterpiece. The story is tense and you get really immersed in it. Trust me, I highly recommend buying this game, it really scratched the story-based game itch I've had for a good while.

Orwell is a mass surveillance sim in which you investigate a series of bombing incidents by following a string of suspects, reading their emails, recording their phone calls, and of course hacking their computers and cell phones, with of course a generous dose of general media research (papers, web publications) 

The game mechanics, were interesting most of the time, as it was somehow convincing that you were actually doing that kind of work, but at certain points it felt short and disappointing , maybe because of a small budget or maybe because limitations. For example the game lacked voices when recording phone calls (instead of using just text all the time), which would've been more dramatic (especially for certain parts) and made more sense since you are recording voices, also the game lacked more scenes in which you actually can see something happening. 
Even if you are a special agent in a remote location, physically detached from the place and you are watching things from a distance, it’s not so rare these days to have easy access through the web to voices recordings and videos whether be news or surveillance cams so it kind of ends up being short of realism and not that exciting. I suppose these really was a budget limitation more than a creative decision, especially because the story ends up being intricate and interesting.

I would admit that the context of what is happening in the game is something not close to me (luckily I don't have recurring bombings in my country as a way of protest) so I didn't feel attached to the general story, but it was the interaction between the different characters, and their personal stories that got me hooked and made more interested as I was playing and advancing the story until the very end. 

It was also of very special interest to me, to see how reality is perceived through a very tiny lens sometimes, and how one person's judgment could be potentially wrong about something. Understanding of things and self images can be manipulated and changed so drastically if we want to, so in a way I consider Orwell a success in showing me how the public perception can be molded and changed. And of course how appropriate the title name is to the game.

If you like puzzle, mystery and crime solving games, then this game is for you!
"But what is different with this game when compared to other games in the same genre?"
Well, Orwell puts you in a human researcher's perspective. As a researcher you have the power to spy on suspects freely, and choose what info should appear in their profile, even if unnecessary.
Be careful, however, because people WILL die if you make the wrong choices (but hey, at least you get achievements for this). Everything has consequences.
The gameplay is simple and you can get into this game easily (if you know how to read).
The story is thrilling and entertaining. The tension when you see a new article after you've done a wrong choice is great.
I recommend this game to anyone that is a fan of these genres, or for people that have never played a game like this and want to get into this.

I had my eye on Orwell for quite some time. It looked intriguing; the whole concept of 24 hour constant surveillance isn't that far fetched, if at all, as much as many of us want to believe otherwise. It sat in my wishlist for a while, then it popped up in a Humble Bundle. It sat for a while in my library, then the free episode came up, and reminded me that I owned the game. Might as well give a whirl, yeah?

At first I was enthralled. They built a small universe that was only a hop, skip, and step away from the one I'm familiar with (good ol' US of A), and I was immediately taken in. I went through the first episode dutifully following along, reading everything I could get my hands on in the game. I combed through the info and made sure the data I supplied was tip-top. I finished out the first day (level) and felt good. Then the second day started.

It was the same thing, except I had a couple other targets to watch. I felt like I had already exhausted the gameplay. Find highlighted text, decide whether or not you want it, drag to box. Occasionally switch box from one character to another (which really just become pedantic when you end up only dealing with five or so interconnected characters). There's no real risk unless you just mean to do poorly, if its even possible. You can't really miss anything, so you never have to juggle the lives of all your surveillance targets. Their web-entries, conversation over text and "phone calls" (just more text doesn't read like a real conversation), will patiently wait for you while you sift through all of it. It gets to the point where you're just hunting highlighted words, as if Orwell has already solved the case on its own. Overall, the game is a bit of a dissappointment, which I only finished to see how the story unfolds. You get a few choices, but there is little in the way of making you feel like you had an impact unless you really got into the story.

TL:DR: All in all, the game is repetitive and after playing through the first episode, I really couldn't recommend purchasing the second one unless you really want to continue the story. I can tell the game was a labor of love, but it just doesn't offer any truly unique insights into the surveillance state and the ethical considerations that surround it, let alone the gameplay.

[h1]Overall Rating[/h1] 
[b]★★☆☆☆[/b]

[u]What I liked[/u]
[list]
  [*] The Story
  [*] The Character Building
[/list]

[u]What I didn't like[/u]
[list]
  [*] The UI/UX
  [*] The Gameplay 
  [*] The replayability 
[/list]

[h1]Review[/h1]

 In Orwell you are an investigator, you need to investigate what might be a terrorist attack, and find the culprit(s). You can check people's background, access their emails, listen to their phone conversations or access their electronic devices. You can choose not to inform what you find to orwell or frame someone so he or she goes to jail.
 There are a couple of different endings, for both the story and the characters (including you, of course). Not all are happy.

[u]Why I liked[/u]
[list]
  [*] The Story: Is really rich, and depending on your choices, full of plot twists.
  [*] The Character Building: All the characters are really well written, how they interact between each other, and their personalities. I in part, what makes the story rich
[/list]

[u]Why didn't like[/u]
[list]
  [*] The UI/UX: You have an annoying companion, that cannot be disabled, that makes annoying comments about the data you upload. The uploading process could be faster also, I understand it tries to simulate a real computer connected to internet, but still it could be faster.
  [*] The Gameplay: Even though your choices matter, there are not a lot of choices you can make. All the data-chunks get highlighted, and the only options you have, are either uploading the information, or not. There's really no challenge, and probably by the third episode, you'll just be looking for highlighted text.
  [*] The replayability: I got all the Achievements in about 28 hours, and completed the game 4 times in that time, exploring all the endings.
[/list]

[h1]Bottom Line[h1]
 I thought I was going to find something different, something I could replay once and again. I really think the game has a lot of potential, but I can't recommend it.

I got the game for free from the humble store. I've never heard about this game before but it is a really interesting experience. You are an investigator that is testing a new system called ORWELL (of course that's a reference to "1984" a famous novel by George Orwell). The system basically gives you access to every possible information about a person. You can access chat logs, private conversations, e-mails. You can even directly access their phones or computers if you get their ID number. The plot is pretty simple at the beggining but it gets really interesting at the end because it asks important questions about how we can lose basically all of our privacy because of really fast development of security systems and the government need of keeping us under control. Lowering the crime rate at the cost of our privacy and things like that. The gameplay is all about reading e-mails and conversations to find information relevant to the terrorist attacks so it may seem boring but once you get into the story you just want to know what's gonna happen next and you keep playing. The game is really short and that's good cause the gameplay would probably be boring if the game was any longer. The game also has multiple endings so if you you don't have enough after your first playthrough you can always replay the game. If you like games with good and interesting plot i highly recommend you try it out. And if you also got the game for free but just didn't have time to play it just give it a chance. It will definitely be worth your while.

The ending(s) are mostly anti-survellance, infact it's pretty hard to end the game without mass revolt and having orwell cancelled, even though it's succesful in saving lives. I enjoyed datamining my punk a$$ subjects and was really pissed off when three of my subjects got away with litteral crimes even though I had evidence against all of them. 

As I'm writing this I want to chance my answer to 'not recommend' but the game was damn fun to play and I'd like more people to learn about datamining, manipulation, forming opinions and how to be impartial. A good 6.5/10

While a good concept in reality, and not awfully executed, I find this game has two pretty blatant flaws. The narrative -  at least the little of what I experienced - seems very on the nose. As in, there is no subtly to the story they are trying to tell. Secondly, there is a fatal flaw in the game mechanic. 

The main mechanic is dragging information into a profile of someone to build up a profile of them. Fine and all, but there's two parts to the fatal flaw. Number one: You can't undo dragging in info. New info can overwrite previous info, but you cannot erase something. Secondly, context is not taken into account. During one portion I dragged in a comment from what was effectively facebook which contained a very obvious hyperbolic joke, and the profiler took it as literal and your helper agent freaked out at what the info was. This little thing absolutely killed the game for me. Without context, a way to edit it, or erase this clearly false information, the game is actively working against you when you try to profile people. The obvious counter point is 'Well the game gave you tips not to just drag in information willy nilly', but the fact it BLATANTLY ignores any context that the player sees is ridiculous.

This isn't a bad game, but between a very shallow seeming plot that basically could just be called 'The CIA watches UC Berkeley commits a Riot' and a picky core - no, let me rephrase that - ONLY mechanic, this isn't an experience I wanted to continue playing.

This is a game I highly recommend if:

- You're looking for a short but solid game with multiple endings and choices that matter (big and small)
- You're concerned at all by privacy, especially online
- You enjoy stories about surveillance and espionage
- You want to live out your fantasies of working for the NSA or any of your favorite intelligence alphabet agencies
- You are a Person of Interest fan who wants to roleplay as Samaritan

Although Orwell is a story of fiction, the elements it presents are believable and much closer to reality than one might expect. Do try out the free demo to see if it's something you might enjoy; if you do, buying the full game and all five episodes is definitely worth it.

This is the game where you play a bad NSA Agent.

So, this is a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure game, where you are investigating documents, pulling important and not-so important information out to further your investigations, and then making choices between conflicting chunks of information to feed into the system.
The truth you present to the investigation is what drives the story, and otherwise the story is told through newpaper articles, message feeds and other pictures and documents.

The animation in the trailer? That occurs solely within the intro sequence of the game and is not gameplay.
Just FYI.

There is no save system, which is a pity. Putting your fingers between the pages of a CYOA is half the fun, as how else are you meant to see all the endings. This game expects that you will instead play through multiple times for minor differences.

That said, the story is solid, and is to all intents and purposes how these monitoring systems would work in real life.
Namely, an investigation is launched on an individual, you'd search their records off the database based on selected metadata, and then the investigation will spread to related individuals based on a third party's incomplete perspective of the scenario.

This game rather heavily leans on the 'incomplete' perspective however, and more documents only become available to you after you've passed critical choices that may have wanted to rely on this information. It feels like the game is cheating here, as the context is missing on the first playthrough and so the consequence of your actions is not clear. Much like when you turn to page 76 of a CYOA and your gnarly motorcycle jump has your character land in the gaping maw of a space turtle and hideously die.

Not sure if this is still free.
Pick it up if it is; the story is very solid, and all else yields to it.

Otherwise still very good for one playthrough, if short.
Won't be repeating content just to get a different ending.

I recieved this game for free on Humble Bundle.

Without spoiling the plot too much, I'll sum it up this way: You play a person who applied to a super secret government survelliance program called Orwell, which had to launch early (again, in secret) due to a terrorist attack. You job is to monitor persons of interests through their text messages, email, phone calls, bank accounts, and doing your own research about them online. You upload information about them to Orwell, and your 'boss' talks you through the investigation.

The story is great, and it will keep you guessing until the end. It's worth playing for the story alone.

That all said, I felt the game was very much hand-holdy. The information you have to drag-and-drop into Orwell in order to advance the story is highlighted for you. It isn't until you get very late into the game that the information you upload could have a negative effect on your investigation. Until you get to that point, however, you might get a snarky remark about uploaded irrelevant information bits (which there are very few) but that's it. 

I would have preferred if the information wasn't highlighted and I had to dig it up myself and put it into Orwell. I'd really feel like a true investigator if that were the case, but I can understand why a small indie studio isn't able to accomplish that.

It's a short game. I completed it in about 4 hours. I don't see much replayability with this game, unfortunately. I was a little disappointed there wasn't a second story to play through or something like that. (Though I did learn there is a 'second episode' available, which I haven't checked out yet due to other games coming out that I want to purchase)

If you like a game with a really good story, drop the 10 bucks and get this game. Even with the complaints I listed above, I found this game enjoyable and would recommend it.

As much as I admire technical aspects and writing in the game, I strongly recommend you to avoid buying it. The game tells a modern story about a survelliance state. This is a divisive and complicated topic. It would have been nice if the game went though the pros and cons of survelliance and then let the player decide on their own.

Instead, the game's message is one-sided and biased: "Survelliance is bad, BAD, BAAD; it's a corrupt tool built by corrupt people, therefore BURN IT". I'm very sad to see such treatment. It is a very dangerous message. I'm not saying survelliance is a shining white knight of good, but it's not a dark super-villain either. Like any thing in life it's shades of grey, and everyone has to decide on their own. The game does not let you to. It pretends to, but gives you a choice between a few shades of black instead.
